**The three explicit confirmations you asked for:**

1. **No endpoint or code path anywhere in this repo writes to warden-contract.** The indexer only calls getEvents (a read) against Soroban RPC. Every HTTP route (/summary, /timeseries, /wallet/:address/events) is GET\-only — anything else gets 405. Verified by reading routes.ts end to end: no mutating contract call exists anywhere in indexer/.  
2. **Current policy/velocity on the wallet drill-down page is a live warden-sdk read, never the indexer's cache.** WalletDrilldown.tsx calls wardenClient.getPolicy/wardenClient.getVelocity directly on every page load; only the *historical* evaluation list comes from the indexer's /wallet/:address/events. Tested explicitly (the "no policy set" test renders getPolicy returning null live, independent of any indexed history).  
3. **The retention-window guard actually warns rather than silently showing gaps as complete.** poller.ts compares the wanted resume ledger against the RPC response's own oldestLedger every cycle and console.warns RETENTION GAP when they don't line up — verified by a dedicated test (warns loudly when the wanted ledger has aged out of RPC retention), not just asserted in prose.

**One correctness point worth flagging:** before writing the decoder, I generated real on-chain events against the live deployed contract (a set\_policy and an evaluate that triggers stepup\_req) and fetched them back through getEvents \+ scValToNative to see the actual decoded shapes rather than assume them from the Rust source. Two things weren't obvious from the spec: amounts decode to strings already (not raw XDR needing manual parsing), and StepUpReason's unit-variant enum decodes as a single-element array (\["NewRecipient"\]), not a bare string — handled correctly in eventDecoder.ts, with the real captured example in the code comment.

## **3\. Repo-relationship description**

> Warden is four repos with a strict, one-directional dependency chain: warden-contract → warden-sdk → warden-app / warden-monitor. warden-contract is a Soroban smart contract and the *only* place the allow/step-up decision is made — it stores per-wallet policy and spending velocity, and returns a decision when asked. warden-sdk is a TypeScript client library that wraps every contract call in a build-unsigned-transaction/submit-signed-transaction pair; it never signs anything itself and holds no private key. warden-app, a Next.js reference wallet, depends on warden-sdk for every read and write to the contract, and adds WebAuthn passkey signing on top. warden-monitor also depends on warden-sdk — its dashboard uses it for live policy/velocity reads — but its indexer talks to Soroban RPC directly to poll on-chain events into its own SQLite store, and has no write path back to the contract anywhere in its code. No repo below warden-contract in this chain is permitted to make or override the allow/step-up decision; that rule is enforced by convention and stated explicitly in every repo's own documentation, not by any technical barrier beyond the contract being the only place evaluate() exists.

## **4\. Planned issues description**

> 14 scoped issues are open across the four repos right now, each with acceptance criteria and a complexity label, not placeholders. warden-contract (4 issues) tracks the real next step for cryptographic step-up enforcement — registering the contract as a genuine smart-wallet policy signer, which the current v1 deliberately defers — plus a sliding velocity window, surfacing multiple simultaneous step-up reasons, and commissioning a third-party audit before any Mainnet use. warden-sdk (3 issues) tracks publishing to npm, adding live-network integration tests to catch what mocked unit tests structurally can't (a real signing bug shipped in v0.1.2 despite 34 passing unit tests, found only by running the SDK against the live contract), and a coordinated change once the contract's step-up-reason issue lands. warden-app (4 issues) tracks the Vercel deployment, the same policy-signer work coordinated with warden-contract's issue, replacing its current single-deployer-key transaction co-signing with real fee-sponsorship infrastructure, and adding Playwright end-to-end tests with a WebAuthn virtual authenticator. warden-monitor (3 issues) tracks deploying the indexer to Render and the dashboard to Vercel, and turning its retention-window gap warning from a log line into a real alert. Several of these carry explicit cross-repo "Depends on" references rather than being scoped in isolation.

## **5\. Project description (submission form)**

> Warden is an open-source risk-policy engine for Stellar smart wallets that decides, per transaction, whether a transfer can proceed on the wallet's ordinary signature alone or needs a second explicit confirmation — based on the amount, whether the recipient is trusted, and how much the wallet has already spent in the last 24 hours. It exists because embedded-wallet apps today apply the same authentication friction to every action regardless of size — a real user of a Nigerian fintech app wrote that they "had to move all my funds out immediately" after being unable to turn off face-scan confirmation for every single action — while the opposite failure, no friction on a large transfer to a new address, is how account takeovers actually happen. Warden targets that middle ground. It's built on Stellar specifically because Soroban smart wallets evaluate multiple signers with distinct roles inside the wallet's own authorization check, which lets the allow/step-up decision live on-chain at the same trust boundary as the wallet itself, rather than in a backend service a wallet provider has to separately build, run, and trust.

Two different things here — a real bug, and a real product-design disagreement. Let me take them separately.

**On Freighter vs. what's actually built:** This isn't a bug — it's the architecture the project was built to. Warden creates a **Soroban smart wallet with a WebAuthn passkey** (Windows Hello, Face ID, fingerprint) as the signer, not a Freighter-style browser extension with a seed phrase. That was a deliberate choice from the master brief: the whole point of a passkey smart wallet is no seed phrase, no extension, sign with your fingerprint. Freighter is the *other*, older Stellar wallet model — different signer entirely. I can add Freighter as an alternative connect option if that's actually what you want for this demo, but that's a real scope decision, not something I should just swap in silently.

**On "Passkey registration failed":** That's a real bug — the button doesn't work, and I need to fix it, not explain it away. That message is coming straight from passkey-kit's own internal error, so I need the actual detail behind it. Can you:

\# Warden Frontend: Verified Open-Source GitHub Reference Library

&nbsp;

\#\# TL;DR

\- \*\*You can build Warden almost entirely from verified open-source parts\*\*: the highest-leverage anchors are \`nateherkai/scroll-craft\` (a Claude Code skill purpose-built for premium scroll-driven sites, 2.3k stars / 341 forks, MIT), \`tremorlabs/tremor\` \+ Recharts/visx for dark financial charts, \`Creit-Tech/Stellar-Wallets-Kit\` and \`stellar/passkey-kit\` for wallet-connect/signing UX, \`paper-design/shaders\` for a zero-dependency shader hero, and \`ateliertriay/bricolage\` (OFL-1.1) for your display typeface — all confirmed live as of Sep 2026\.

\- \*\*Avoid the generic-template trap by treating templates as structure, not skin\*\*: pull layout/architecture from shadcn-based admin starters (satnaing/shadcn-admin, Kiranism/next-shadcn-dashboard-starter) but replace their color tokens, fonts, and iconography with your jade/amber scheme, Bricolage/Instrument pairing, and a custom threshold-gate motif rendered as SVG/shader rather than any stock illustration pack.

\- \*\*A few "plausible" repos could not be fully verified\*\* (exact stars/license on some low-profile Stellar demo repos and the Trustless Work blocks library); these are flagged explicitly below rather than presented as confirmed.

&nbsp;

\#\# Key Findings

\- The Stellar/Soroban front-end ecosystem is small but real and directly relevant: \`stellar/passkey-kit\` (active home; the old \`kalepail/passkey-kit\` was archived Jul 31, 2026 and its banner explicitly points there), \`Creit-Tech/Stellar-Wallets-Kit\` (the multi-wallet connector, NOT under the \`stellar\` org), and Trustless Work's React "blocks" library give you production-tested connect \+ transaction-signing flows to copy.

\- For distinctive (non-"AI template") visuals, the strongest open-source anchors are \`nateherkai/scroll-craft\`, \`paper-design/shaders\`, \`darkroomengineering/lenis\`, and the now-fully-free GSAP toolset (GSAP became free with its 3.13 release announced May 6, 2025 — "100% free including all of the bonus plugins like SplitText, MorphSVG ... even for commercial use"; current npm version 3.15.0 under the "Standard no charge" license).

\- Your exact type pairing is fully open-source: Bricolage Grotesque (OFL-1.1, \`ateliertriay/bricolage\`, by Mathieu Triay) and Instrument Sans (OFL, by Rodrigo Fuenzalida, on Google Fonts) — both installable via Fontsource for self-hosting.

\- The jade-green/amber (Allow / Step-up) scheme and threshold-gate motif have no off-the-shelf repo; you must implement these as custom Tailwind tokens \+ custom SVG/shader, using geometric-pattern libraries (geo\_pattern, svg-patterns) rather than character-illustration packs.

&nbsp;

\#\# Details

&nbsp;

\#\#\# Category 1 — Full UI kit / design-system starters (React \+ Tailwind \+ TS, dark, fintech)

\#\# Recommendations

\*\*Stage 1 — Scaffold the app shell (week 1).\*\* Fork \`satnaing/shadcn-admin\` (or \`Kiranism/next-shadcn-dashboard-starter\` if you want Next.js App Router) for the authenticated dashboard, policy-settings, and transaction screens. Immediately override: (a) Tailwind color tokens to ink \`\#101728\` \+ jade "Allow" \+ amber "Step-up"; (b) fonts to Bricolage Grotesque (display) / Instrument Sans (body) via Fontsource; (c) icons — keep Lucide as base, add Phosphor/Tabler for the gate motif. Benchmark to change course: if the reskinned shell still "reads generic" after token/font/icon swaps, add Tremor cards \+ a bespoke visx velocity gauge to break the grid.

&nbsp;

\*\*Stage 2 — Charts (week 1–2).\*\* Use \`tremorlabs/tremor\` for fast dark KPI cards \+ time-series, and drop to \`airbnb/visx\` for the one signature viz (a threshold/step chart that literally embodies the gate motif). Custom-style Recharts tooltips (paigen11 reference) if you prefer Recharts. Threshold: if a chart needs a non-standard shape (gate/step band), that's your signal to use visx rather than Tremor/Recharts.

&nbsp;

\*\*Stage 3 — Landing hero (week 2).\*\* Install \`nateherkai/scroll-craft\` as a Claude Code plugin and let it drive the scroll-driven hero, paired with \`darkroomengineering/lenis\` \+ free GSAP ScrollTrigger. For the interactive shader element, use \`@paper-design/shaders-react\` (mesh gradient in ink/jade) and consider \`paper-design/liquid-logo\` for the animated Warden mark. Use \`creativoma/lenis-gsap-lab\` as the mechanics reference. Threshold: if scroll-craft's output collides with its own "uniqueness registry," pick a different grammar it suggests rather than fighting it.

&nbsp;

\*\*Stage 4 — Wallet \+ signing UX (week 2–3).\*\* Wire \`Creit-Tech/Stellar-Wallets-Kit\` for the connect modal and \`stellar/passkey-kit\` for passkey smart-wallet signing. Copy transaction-signing UX patterns from \`stellar/soroban-react-payment\` and \`kalepail/soroban-passkey\`; copy escrow/policy-display patterns from \`Trustless-Work/escrow-viewer\` and the \`react-library-trustless-work-blocks\` library. Threshold: if you need multi-wallet support beyond Freighter, Stellar Wallets Kit is mandatory; if passkey-only, passkey-kit alone suffices.

&nbsp;

\*\*Stage 5 — Motif \+ polish.\*\* Build the threshold-gate identity as custom SVG (optionally generated/seeded via \`derhuerst/svg-patterns\` or \`geo\_pattern\`) and animate state transitions with \`rive-app/rive-react\` or Lottie via \`LottieFiles/dotlottie-web\`. Avoid all excluded stock illustration packs.

1\. UI kit/shell → \*\*satnaing/shadcn-admin\*\*

2\. Landing/scroll hero → \*\*nateherkai/scroll-craft\*\*

3\. Financial dashboard template → \*\*stellar/stellar-disbursement-platform-frontend\*\* (on-domain) or \*\*Trustless-Work/escrow-viewer\*\*

4\. Charts → \*\*tremorlabs/tremor\*\* (fast) \+ \*\*airbnb/visx\*\* (signature viz)

5\. Shader hero → \*\*paper-design/shaders\*\*

6\. Motion → \*\*darkroomengineering/lenis\*\* \+ free \*\*GSAP\*\*

7\. Geometric illustration/pattern → \*\*jasonlong/geo\_pattern\*\* / \*\*derhuerst/svg-patterns\*\*

8\. Fonts → \*\*ateliertriay/bricolage\*\* \+ Instrument Sans via \*\*fontsource\*\*

9\. Stellar wallet/signing → \*\*Creit-Tech/Stellar-Wallets-Kit\*\* \+ \*\*stellar/passkey-kit\*\*

10\. State-driven illustration → \*\*rive-app/rive-react\*\*

**Two design decisions I made and want to flag explicitly, since the task described the *what* but not every *exactly how*:**

1. **hourly\_velocity\_cap is a new, separately-configured field** (must be ≤ daily\_velocity\_cap), not the existing daily cap reused. The task's own rationale — "catches rapid-fire spending a single daily cap misses" — only holds if the hourly threshold is independently meaningful. Documented in a code comment and the README.  
2. **Map\<Address, u64\>**, not Vec\<(Address, u64)\> — justified in a types.rs comment: evaluate() looks this up by key on every call, which is exactly Map's access pattern; a Vec of tuples would need a linear scan for no benefit, since insertion order is never used.

**The migration note you asked for is real, not boilerplate** — I checked, and it matters concretely: warden-contract's *live Testnet deployment* (CBFQ752...) already holds real policy data under the *old* schema from all our earlier testing. This code hasn't been deployed — deploying it means a **new contract ID**, not an upgrade (no upgrade function exists, by design), and every wallet re-sets its policy from scratch. Documented in the contract's own README and now in DEPLOYMENT-INFO.md too, flagged as an open item so it doesn't get silently forgotten before the next deploy.

Step 1: What to Do Right Now (Immediate Action Plan)

Do not deploy blindly. Follow this 4-step checklist:

&nbsp;

1\. Deploy the New Contract

Have the developer compile and deploy the new code to Stellar Testnet.

&nbsp;

This will generate a New Contract ID (let's call it CNEW...).

&nbsp;

2\. Write a Simple "Mover Truck" Script (Migration Script)

Instead of forcing everyone to manually re-type every wallet limit and policy by hand:

&nbsp;

Write a quick setup script (in TypeScript, Python, or Rust).

&nbsp;

This script should automatically read the test policies you had on the old contract and save them into the new contract CNEW....

&nbsp;

Running this script takes 5 seconds and resets all your test data cleanly.

&nbsp;

3\. Update the Address in Every Project File

Update your environment files (.env) and settings across your entire project:

&nbsp;

Change WARDEN\_CONTRACT\_ID=CBFQ752... to WARDEN\_CONTRACT\_ID=CNEW....

&nbsp;

Update the frontend dashboard, backend APIs, and your automated test suites so they point to the new address.

&nbsp;

4\. "Turn Off the Lights" on the Old Contract

Update DEPLOYMENT-INFO.md and your README.md.

&nbsp;

Clearly mark the old address CBFQ752... as DEPRECATED / RETIRED.

&nbsp;

If the old contract has an administrative toggle or pause switch, disable it so nobody accidentally runs tests against it.

&nbsp;

Step 2: What to Decide Before Launching on Mainnet (The Bigger Question)

This warning revealed a major design choice: Should the Warden contract be immutable (permanent), or should it have an upgrade button?

&nbsp;

There are two ways to handle this in production:

&nbsp;

Path A: Keep It Permanent (No Upgrade Button)

The Good: It gives 100% trust. Big banks and corporate clients love this because it means no rogue developer or hacked admin key can ever silently change the contract rules.

&nbsp;

The Bad: Every time you improve the code or fix a bug in the future, every single user and company has to manually sign a transaction to move their account to a new contract address.

&nbsp;

Path B: Add Soroban's Built-in Upgrade Tool

Stellar Soroban actually has a built-in function called env.deployer().update\_current\_contract\_wasm().

&nbsp;

How it works: It allows an authorized admin or a multi-signature board to swap in new code without changing the contract ID or losing any stored data.

&nbsp;

Recommendation: If you plan to add more AI risk features over the next 6 to 12 months, add a controlled upgrade function now before deploying to Mainnet. You can lock that upgrade function behind a 3-of-5 multi-signature key or Warden's governance, so it stays safe and decentralized while saving you from migration headaches.

&nbsp;

Path C: The "Front Door" Router Pattern

Build a tiny, simple "Front Door" contract that never changes.

&nbsp;

When a user sends a transaction, the Front Door forwards it to "Warden Engine v1."

&nbsp;

When you release "Warden Engine v2," the Front Door simply redirects traffic to the new engine. The user never has to change their wallet settings or learn a new contract address.

&nbsp;

Direct answer: **I'd push back on Path C — it's not actually safer than Path B, and it's more work for the same core risk.** Let me walk through why, then recommend what I think is actually right for where this project is right now.

## **The thing Path B and Path C have in common (and it matters)**

Both are "swap the logic without changing what the user points at." Whether that's env.deployer().update\_current\_contract\_wasm() swapping the WASM in place, or a router contract redirecting calls to a different address — **the trust question is identical: who controls the switch?** A router that can redirect to a new "engine" contract is functionally an upgrade admin, just implemented as an extra hop instead of an in-place swap. Anyone who can flip that router's target can change how every policy decision gets made, for every wallet, silently. That's not a smaller version of Path B's risk — it's the same risk with an extra contract in front of it.

And Path C actually costs more than B for that same risk:

* **Every evaluate() call now makes a cross-contract call** through the router — real added latency and resource fees on every single transaction, forever, not just at upgrade time.  
* **It contradicts something already deliberately decided in this project**: warden-contract's spec explicitly says "no cross-contract calls" and "no admin override of a wallet's own policy" — not as an oversight, but because the whole architectural argument for building this on Stellar is that *the decision lives at the same trust boundary as the wallet itself*, not behind a separately-controlled layer. A router reintroduces exactly the kind of "backend service someone has to separately trust and operate" that the project was built to avoid.  
* **It needs real verification, not assumption**: does require\_auth() behave the same way through a proxied cross-contract call as a direct one? That's a genuine Soroban semantics question I would not want to guess at — proxy patterns are also a well-known source of subtle bugs elsewhere (storage collisions, auth-context confusion) precisely because of this kind of indirection.

## **What I'd actually recommend: Path A, for now, on purpose**

Not because upgradability is bad forever — because of where this project actually is:

* **There are no real users yet.** This is Testnet, submission-stage. The entire cost of "redeploy \= new contract ID" is: you re-run set\_policy for the one test wallet that has data. That's it. This is the cheapest possible moment to pay that cost — it gets more expensive every day real users exist.  
* **Locking in an upgrade mechanism now, without a real governance system**, is worse than no upgrade mechanism. A single admin key or a small ungoverned multisig is a bigger practical risk than "nobody can change it" — you'd be adding a real attack surface to solve a migration-friction problem that doesn't exist yet.  
* **If this reaches real adoption**, the right move isn't a quick router — it's Phase 16's guardian pattern (already designed: proposal \+ approval threshold \+ timelock \+ owner-veto) applied to *governance*, not just wallet recovery. That's a real, deliberately-designed system, not a bolt-on.

## **On your Step 1 checklist — mostly right, two corrections**

1–3 are the right moves once you're ready. One thing to know before you write that migration script: **it can't actually be a silent bulk-migrator.** set\_policy requires the wallet's own signature (wallet.require\_auth()) — no admin can set someone else's policy, by design. A script can *read* every old policy via the public get\_policy and *construct* the right set\_policy calls, but each one still needs that wallet's real key to sign. Since there's currently exactly one real wallet with test data (the deployer identity), writing a whole script is probably overkill — it's faster to just re-run the 2–3 commands directly.

4's "pause switch" doesn't apply — this contract has no admin toggle at all, deliberately (no 8th function, ever). "Turning off the lights" here just means the README/DEPLOYMENT-INFO.md annotation, which I already added when I documented this.

**Want me to proceed with the redeploy under Path A** (new contract ID, no upgrade mechanism, update the env references, mark the old one deprecated), or do you want to keep discussing Path C first?

contract storage decodes by the exact shape the currently-deployed wasm expects — \*\*a

policy stored under the pre-Phase-14 contract cannot be read by this version\*\*, and

there is no in-place upgrade path (this contract deliberately has no admin-upgrade

function, by design — see Scope below).

&nbsp;

Concretely: \`warden-contract\`'s v0.1.0 Testnet deployment

(\`CBFQ752LFNC57U4KWDAEKNU43PLBWJ7M2B4ZRYUMCWL62JHJNUYJVMB5\`) already has real policy

data under the old schema (from earlier testing). Deploying this Phase 14 code means a

\*\*new contract instance, a new contract ID\*\* — not an upgrade of the existing one.

Every wallet, including that Testnet one, needs to call \`set\_policy\` again from

scratch under the new deployment; nothing carries over automatically. This is

acceptable for Testnet with no real funds at stake and no migration tooling built for

v1 — it would not be acceptable for a Mainnet deployment with real user data, which is

exactly the kind of gap a real migration tool or an upgrade mechanism would need to

close before this contract is used for anything beyond Testnet.

export interface PortablePolicyRule {

Fixing warden-sdk for Phase 14 compatibility — necessary to keep warden-app, warden-monitor, and the docs' "actually runs" claim true. This is a real, scoped continuation, not scope creep for its own sake.

**Bash** Update warden-sdk types.ts for Phase 14 fields

IN

wsl.exe \-e bash \-lc "

cd \~/projects/warden-sdk

python3 \- \<\<'PYEOF'

with open('src/types.ts', encoding='utf-8') as f:

    c \= f.read()

&nbsp;

old\_policy \= '''export interface Policy {

  owner: string;

  maxNoStepUp: string;

  dailyVelocityCap: string;

  newRecipientRequiresStepUp: boolean;

  trustedRecipients: string\[\];

  updatedAt: bigint;

}'''

new\_policy \= '''export interface Policy {

  owner: string;

  maxNoStepUp: string;

  dailyVelocityCap: string;

  hourlyVelocityCap: string;

  newRecipientRequiresStepUp: boolean;

  /\*\* Address \-\> last\_paid\_at (ledger timestamp of the most recent transfer

   \* evaluate() saw to this recipient, or when they were added if never

   \* paid since). A plain object, not a Map, since this is decoded straight

   \* from the contract's own Map\<Address, u64\> via the dynamic contract

   \* spec and JSON-serializes cleanly either way. \*/

  trustedRecipients: Record\<string, bigint\>;

  trustDecaySeconds: bigint;

  updatedAt: bigint;

}'''

assert old\_policy in c

c \= c.replace(old\_policy, new\_policy)

&nbsp;

old\_reason \= \\"export type StepUpReason \= 'AmountExceeded' | 'NewRecipient' | 'VelocityExceeded';\\"

new\_reason \= \\"export type StepUpReason \= 'AmountExceeded' | 'NewRecipient' | 'VelocityExceeded' | 'HourlyVelocityExceeded';\\"

assert old\_reason in c

c \= c.replace(old\_reason, new\_reason)

&nbsp;

old\_rule \= '''export interface PortablePolicyRule {

  version: 1;

  maxAmountNoStepUp: string;

  dailyVelocityCap: string;

  newRecipientRequiresStepUp: boolean;

  trustedRecipients: string\[\];

}'''

new\_rule \= '''export interface PortablePolicyRule {

  version: 1;

  maxAmountNoStepUp: string;

  dailyVelocityCap: string;

  newRecipientRequiresStepUp: boolean;

  trustedRecipients: string\[\];

  /\*\* Decimal string, e.g. \\"50.00\\". Must be \<= dailyVelocityCap \-- the

   \* contract rejects otherwise (InvalidPolicyParams). \*/

  hourlyVelocityCap: string;

  /\*\* Duration in seconds a trusted recipient stays trusted without a

   \* payment. A plain number is safe here (realistic decay durations never

   \* approach u64/Number.MAX\_SAFE\_INTEGER); converted to a BigInt at the

   \* contract-call boundary regardless, since that field is u64 on-chain. \*/

  trustDecaySeconds: number;

}'''

assert old\_rule in c

c \= c.replace(old\_rule, new\_rule)

&nbsp;

with open('src/types.ts', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:

    f.write(c)

print('types.ts updated')

PYEOF

"

function decodePolicy(raw: RawPolicy, decimals: number): Policy {

    dailyVelocityCap: i128ToDecimal(raw.daily\_velocity\_cap, decimals),

    newRecipientRequiresStepUp: raw.new\_recipient\_requires\_stepup,

    trustedRecipients: \[...raw.trusted\_recipients\],

    updatedAt: raw.updated\_at,

  };

}'''

&nbsp;

new\_raw \= '''interface RawPolicy {

  owner: string;

  max\_no\_stepup: bigint;

  daily\_velocity\_cap: bigint;

  hourly\_velocity\_cap: bigint;

  new\_recipient\_requires\_stepup: boolean;

  // Decoded from the contract's Map\<Address, u64\> \-- a plain object, not

  // an array. The old shape here (string\[\]) was Phase \<14; this SDK now

  // targets the Phase 14 contract exclusively.

  trusted\_recipients: Record\<string, bigint\>;

  trust\_decay\_seconds: bigint;

  updated\_at: bigint;

}

&nbsp;

function decodePolicy(raw: RawPolicy, decimals: number): Policy {

  return {

    owner: raw.owner,

    maxNoStepUp: i128ToDecimal(raw.max\_no\_stepup, decimals),

    dailyVelocityCap: i128ToDecimal(raw.daily\_velocity\_cap, decimals),

    hourlyVelocityCap: i128ToDecimal(raw.hourly\_velocity\_cap, decimals),

    newRecipientRequiresStepUp: raw.new\_recipient\_requires\_stepup,

    trustedRecipients: { ...raw.trusted\_recipients },

    trustDecaySeconds: raw.trust\_decay\_seconds,

    updatedAt: raw.updated\_at,

  };

}'''
